rationale: B wins because it stress-tests the ugly questions before a reporter does; 'Is the closing plant where this blend is made?' is the line that saves the founder from walking into traffic. A has useful bones, but 'customers who don't specify get oat milk' turns 'default non-dairy option' into a different claim. B still has a surcharge/pricing wobble, but its beats are cleaner, its proof asks are sharper, and its four angles are more structurally distinct.
gaps_in_A: 'customers who don't specify get oat milk' is not in the update. 'Default non-dairy option' does not mean oat milk replaces dairy for customers who say nothing.
'falling volumes, shrinking retail shelf space, canceled expansions' imports a plant-based sector narrative the supplied facts do not prove. That needs external evidence, not confident scenery.
'Customer-story (the coffee chain's procurement decision) - no_journalist_shape' contradicts the kept default-option angle, which also depends on the unnamed chain and a chain-side spokesperson.
It leaves money on the table by mentioning 'no price change at retail' only as a supporting fact instead of testing the cleaner retail-pricing and margin angle.
gaps_in_B: 'default, not the upcharge' overreaches. The update says no retail price change, not that the coffee chain dropped or avoided a non-dairy surcharge.

'The prevailing belief is that unprofitable plant-based companies retreat from sustainability spending' is plausible beat context, but it is not in the supplied facts. Frame it as a question or bring proof.

'Reformulations usually travel with a price move in one direction or the other' is an unsupported premise. The pricing angle is good, but that sentence needs buyer data or it is just PR math in a trench coat.
'I have no current news signal in hand here' is too absolute. The announcement itself supplies a current company-news peg; the fair warning is that there is no broader breaking-news peg.
